_about: The whole walkthrough: the eight stages, and the source note at the foot of
the page. This file is the one to edit for wording and numbers.
sub        second line on the rail card
action     one line on what needs to happen, under the heading
where      where this happens, in plain words
law        what should happen - one string per paragraph
branches   optional sub-outcomes, shown as small cards: {t, b}
myths      [{claim, truth}] - things women were told that are untrue
Paragraphs take inline HTML: <b> for emphasis, and entities such as

stages.title: After an incident of violence
stages.action: You can open a criminal case, apply for a protection order, or do both.
stages.where: A police station or a magistrate's court
law: A survivor can do one of two things, or both. A criminal case can be opened at a police station. An application for a protection order has to be lodged at a magistrate’s court. One action does not cancel the other, and doing one does not mean the other has to be done too.

stages.title: The application is completed and lodged
stages.action: Once you have filled in the application form, you should give it to the court’s clerk, who will register it while you are there.
law: The application form is completed and lodged with the clerk of the court. You must apply yourself — somebody else can’t do it for you — but you may ask for help with the paperwork.
You do not have to apply at a court where the perpetrator lives.

myths.claim: “You have to apply at the court where he lives.”
myths.truth: You do not. In the study, at least one woman was wrongly told so.

stages.title: A magistrate grants an interim order
stages.action: A magistrate reads the application and decides whether to grant a temporary protection order.
stages.where: The magistrate’s court, usually the same day.
law: The magistrate has to consider the application and review the evidence you provided.

stages.title: The order is handed to the respondent
stages.action: The order must be given to the respondent in person by a police officer or a clerk of the court. It is not in force until this happens.
law: An interim protection order does not come into effect until it has been served — that is, until the respondent has been notified in writing and in person. This has to be done by the court or the police, not by you.
Once the respondent has received the notice, the order is in force — even if they destroy the document.

myths.claim: “A man in jail or awaiting trial in a correctional facility cannot be served.”
myths.truth: He can. Several women described court officials telling them otherwise.

myths.claim: “He tore up the order, so it does not count.”
myths.truth: The order takes effect once the respondent has been given the notice, and it stays in force whatever he does to the paper. Some women stopped engaging with the system because they believed this — sometimes after a police officer told them so.

myths.claim: “It will have to be served again, and you will have to pay.”
myths.truth: One woman was told this by a member of the police. Serving a protection order is not something you need to pay for.

stages.title: A date for a court appearance is set
stages.action: The court sets a date on which the magistrate will decide whether the interim order becomes permanent.
law: A hearing date must be given to anyone granted an interim protection order, so the court can consider whether to make it permanent. The respondent has a chance to say why it should not.
The interim order holds until that hearing, unless it is set aside before then for some reason.
The court must confirm that the respondent was aware of the court date. If the court cannot, they must give another date.

stages.title: The court decides whether the order should become permanent
stages.action: Go to the hearing, or tell the court beforehand if you cannot be there.
law: The court decides whether to make the protection order permanent. What happens depends on who appears:

branches.t: The survivor appears or tells the court they can’t be there
branches.b: If you let the court know that you can’t attend the hearing and you ask for another date, the hearing can be moved.

The court must try to find out why. If you were prevented from attending for a valid reason, another date is given. If there is no good reason, or you do not want the order to become permanent, the order lapses.

branches.t: The respondent appears or asks for a postponement
branches.b: The hearing proceeds or is moved to a new date.

branches.t: The respondent neither appears nor lets the court know that they can’t attend
branches.b: The court must first confirm that the respondent was aware of the date. If they were, the hearing can go ahead without them.

stages.title: The final order is granted
stages.action: The magistrate makes the order permanent if satisfied that there is evidence of abuse.
law: The magistrate grants a final protection order if convinced there is evidence of domestic abuse. If not — or if the interim order has lapsed — the original protection order is no longer valid.
Three further provisions can be asked for:

branches.b: This allows the police to check on you for some time if you still live with your partner.
This can be applied for once an order is granted.
This lets you recover costs you have already carried.

stages.title: If the rules are disobeyed
stages.action: Tell the police that the rules of the order have been broken and ask them for an arrest.
law: A breach of a protection order is a criminal matter. The survivor can ask the police to arrest the perpetrator.

source.label: Source:
source.citation: Jewkes R, Ramsoomar L, Chirwa E, et al 2026 Protection orders protect many women from Intimate Partner Violence (IPV): findings from four provincial sites in South Africa SAMRC Evidence brief, Pretoria.
